long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, II.C Summary of Major Provisions p 40678; IV.B Definitions p 40692-40693]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS proposes to block the program from fraud and threats to national security. Congress gave USCIS new powers in INA 203(b)(5)(N) and (O). Under the proposal, if a petition, application or benefit is found to be based on fraud, deceit, intentional material misrepresentation or criminal misuse, USCIS can deny, suspend, debar or terminate regional centers, NCEs and JCEs and deny petitions [FR 2026-13392, II.C Summary of Major Provisions, p 40678]. Fraud is defined as knowingly making a false statement or hiding a material fact to induce action. Examples include Ponzi schemes, falsifying job creation, fake source of funds, fake family members [FR 2026-13392, IV.B Definitions - Fraud / Deceit / Criminal Misuse, p 40692-40693].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Fraud, criminal misuse and national security bars
long_summary_by_theme.uscis_phrasing: Implementing sections 203(b)(5)(N) and (O) of the INA to protect the EB-5 program from fraud and threats to national security

long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS would reorganize EB-5 rules into a new subpart D and add definitions for things like certifier, comprehensive business plan, debar, suspend, terminate, direct jobs, indirect jobs, criminal misuse, fraud, deceit [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678; IV.B Definitions p 40691-40694]. Certifier now includes promoters registered under INA 203(b)(5)(H)(i). A comprehensive business plan must still be credible and include nature, timeline, size of activity, use of investor capital to create 10 jobs per investor, sources and uses of funds, marketing plan, market analysis, permits, hiring timetable, construction schedule, org structure [FR 2026-13392, IV.B Comprehensive Business Plan, p 40691].
long_summary_by_theme.title: New definitions and who counts as involved

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, II.C Summary of Major Provisions, p 40678]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS proposes to implement RIA priority date retention. An investor who filed a prior EB-5 petition that was approved or not denied for fraud can keep that filing date when filing a new petition, with limits for fraud, national security and material misrepresentation [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Priority date retention

long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: The proposal codifies the current RIA amounts: $1,050,000 standard and $800,000 for TEA or infrastructure, with automatic inflation adjustments starting Jan 1 2027 and every 5 years after [FR 2026-13392, BAL summary cited; II.C p 40678]. For sustainment, RIA changed INA 203(b)(5)(A)(ii) and 216A(d)(1)(A)(ii) to say investment must be expected to remain invested for no less than 2 years. USCIS says since RIA it has interpreted that 2-year clock to start when full qualifying investment is contributed to NCE and placed at risk and made available to JCE [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.6 Duration of Investment, p 40705]. Under proposal, an investor can invest anytime before filing, but investment must be at risk and available to JCE on the date the I-526/E is filed, so USCIS can verify it [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.6, p 40706, proposed 8 CFR 204.407(b)(1)-(3)]. If capital is in escrow pending approval, the 2-year expectation starts after release to job-creating activity [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.6, p 40706].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Investment amount and how long money must stay invested

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7 Job Creation and Bridge Financing, p 40706-40707]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS proposes to eliminate use of repaid bridge financing as a way to show job creation. Bridge financing is a short-term loan used to cover costs until permanent financing arrives [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7 citing Black's Law Dictionary, p 40707]. Previously USCIS allowed it under its 2016 Policy Manual. RIA changed INA 203(b)(5)(A)(ii) from benefit the economy 'and' create jobs to 'by' creating jobs. USCIS reads this as Congress wanting a closer link between the investor's money and the jobs [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7, p 40707]. Proposed 8 CFR 204.407(e)(1) would require job creation be tied to investor capital, and capital must be provided to the entity most closely responsible for creating the employment and used in that activity [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7, p 40706-40707].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Bridge financing eliminated

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, IV.B Direct/Indirect Jobs p 40694; IV.D.7 p 40707]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: An investor must still create 10 jobs. For regional centers, only up to 90% of jobs can be indirect jobs. At least 10% must be direct jobs, which can include employees of the JCE, not just NCE [FR 2026-13392, IV.B Direct Jobs and Indirect Jobs, p 40694]. If construction jobs are less than 2 years, only up to 75% can be indirect and direct construction jobs are prorated [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7, p 40707, proposed 8 CFR 204.407(e)(3)(ii)]. Regional center investors rely on the regional center project application to prove job creation by submitting an economically and statistically valid transparent economic impact analysis [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.7, p 40707].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Job creation counting

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, I. Public Participation B and C, p 40677; II.C]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS proposes to describe how high-unemployment TEAs are designated, including what data sources to use for weighted unemployment average of census tracts, and how a regional center should renew a previously designated high-unemployment area under INA 203(b)(5)(B)(ii)(IV) [FR 2026-13392, I. Public Participation C, p 40677]. USCIS is also asking for comment on what types of projects meet the definition of infrastructure project [FR 2026-13392, I. Public Participation B, p 40677]. Investment thresholds for TEA/infrastructure remain $800k now, subject to inflation adjustments [FR 2026-13392, II.C].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Targeted employment area and infrastructure projects

long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: Previously an investor could qualify by investing in a troubled business and preserving jobs. USCIS proposes to remove that as an avenue to establish eligibility [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678; IV.G Troubled Businesses].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Removal of troubled business as eligibility path

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, I. Public Participation A, D, E p 40677; II.C p 40678; IV.B Debar/Suspend/Terminate p 40693]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: RIA added new compliance for regional centers. USCIS proposes rules for designation, project applications (I-956F), redeployment under INA 203(b)(5)(F)(v), bona fides of persons involved under 203(b)(5)(H) [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678; I. Public Participation D and E, p 40677]. USCIS also asks for comment on audits and record-keeping under 203(b)(5)(E)(vii), what records a regional center must keep and how USCIS would audit [FR 2026-13392, I.A p 40677], and how to register direct and third-party promoters [FR 2026-13392, I.E p 40677; II.C]. Enforcement tools include monetary penalties, suspension, debarment and termination under INA 203(b)(5)(G)(iii)(II), (K)(ii), (N), (O) [FR 2026-13392, II.C; IV.B Debar/Suspend/Terminate p 40693]. Statutory integrity fees, reporting and site visits also apply per BAL summary.
long_summary_by_theme.title: Regional center, NCE, JCE compliance, audits and promoter registration

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.4-5 Source of Capital and Digital Assets, p 40704-40705]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: Regional centers must identify all sources of non-EB-5 capital to NCE/JCE, and if USCIS has reason to believe capital is not lawfully derived, it can request evidence [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.4-5, p 40704-40705]. USCIS considered digital assets like cryptocurrency and tokens. It says intangible digital assets can't be directly invested as capital under INA 203(b)(5)(D)(ii), but their conversion to cash may be permissible if lawful source and path are shown with full transaction history, ownership at all times, tax consistency and lawful operation [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.5 Digital Assets, p 40705]. USCIS proposes not to put digital-asset-specific evidentiary rules in regulation yet, but to issue sub-regulatory guidance [FR 2026-13392, IV.D.5 p 40705].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Source and path of funds, including digital assets

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, II.C bullet Creating process improvements for removal of conditions p 40678; IV.I]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: For investors with conditional residence under INA 216A, USCIS proposes process improvements for removing conditions on permanent residence under 8 CFR 216.6, and a new process for amending the I-829 when the regional center is terminated or NCE/JCE debarred [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678]. Investment must have been sustained for 2 years as measured above when USCIS adjudicates I-829 [FR 2026-13392, IV.I].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Removal of conditions on green card

long_summary_by_theme.citation: [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678; IV.J Withdrawal and IV.K Severability]
long_summary_by_theme.plain_text: USCIS proposes to clarify how withdrawal requests are processed and when petitions are automatically revoked, and includes a severability clause so if one provision is struck the rest stands [FR 2026-13392, II.C p 40678, IV.J-K].
long_summary_by_theme.title: Withdrawal, automatic revocation and severability

plain_language_note: Plain-language paraphrases of USCIS NPRM text. Every statement cites the Federal Register section it paraphrases. Unbiased summary, not legal advice. For full text, see source_url.

short_summary.text: On July 2 2026, USCIS proposed rules to implement the EB-5 Reform and Integrity Act of 2022 (RIA), signed March 15 2022. The EB-5 category lets a foreign investor apply for a US green card if they invest required capital in a new commercial enterprise and that investment creates 10 full-time jobs for US workers [FR 2026-13392, Summary, p 40676]. The RIA added fraud, national security, and Regional Center oversight rules. USCIS now proposes to put those into regulation in 8 CFR [FR 2026-13392, II.A Purpose, p 40677]. Comments are due August 31 2026 via regulations.gov docket USCIS-2026-0100 [FR 2026-13392, DATES, p 40676]. Most provisions would apply only to petitions filed on or after the final rule effective date [BAL summary of NPRM scope, 2026].
short_summary.title: What this proposal is

source_document: Federal Register Vol 91 No 126 July 2 2026, FR Doc 2026-13392, 8 CFR Parts 204,205,216,235 [CIS No 2770-24; RIN 1615-AC94]

why_comment.title: Why comment — why it matters for investors
why_comment.intro: This is the first major rule to turn the EB-5 Reform and Integrity Act of 2022 into actual regulations. USCIS published it July 2, 2026 as a 358-page proposal touching nearly every part of EB-5 and is taking comments through August 31, 2026.
citations_intro: [FR 2026-13392, Vol 91 No 126 July 2 2026; IMI: 358-page document implementing RIA, comment period 60 days through Aug 31 2026]

reasons.title: First executable rule for the RIA
reasons.text: Congress passed the RIA in March 2022. This NPRM is the first time USCIS writes those reforms into regulation. Much codifies what Congress decided, but several parts like a new $1.4M tier for high-employment areas and a tiered penalty system are USCIS's own design.
citations: IMI: Much of it writes into regulation what Congress decided in 2022, but several provisions are DHS's own design [IMI 2026]
[FR 2026-13392, IV.B definitions; II.C summary]

reasons.title: Impacts both existing and future investors
reasons.text: Most provisions apply only to petitions filed after the final rule takes effect, but some questions at I-829 like job rules, bridge loan treatment, and sustainment directly affect people who already filed and are waiting on conditional residence. The proposal asks how redeployment, source-of-funds proof for every dollar, and audits work for already-approved projects.
citations: BAL: Most provisions would apply prospectively [BAL 2026]
[FR IV.D.7; IV.D.6; IV.G]

reasons.title: Decides money, jobs, and protections you rely on
reasons.text: The rule locks in investment thresholds ($800K TEA/infrastructure, $1.05M standard) with inflation from Jan 1 2027, a 2-year sustainment clock starting when capital reaches the job company not when your visa is current, ending repaid bridge financing for job creation, capping indirect jobs at 90% and construction indirect at 75%, and spells out what happens if your regional center is terminated — 180-day window to re-associate, keeping priority date, and whether you must lift a finger if you already did 2 years and jobs.
citations: IMI: protections when RC fails 180-day window, priority dates survive [IMI 2026]

reasons.title: Your real experience fills gaps agency asks about
reasons.text: USCIS explicitly asks for comment on what counts as infrastructure, what data should prove high-unemployment TEAs, how to measure weighted unemployment, what records to keep for audits, how fund administrators actually sign on bank accounts, and whether compliance costs are really $47K per center per year. Real numbers from investors and small centers correct the estimate hardest on small single-project centers.
citations: [FR I. Public Participation B, C, A, E p 40677]
IMI: compliance cost $47K estimate, real cost higher, small centers hit hardest [IMI]

reasons.title: Comments create a record the agency must consider
reasons.text: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal agency must publish the proposal, explain its reasoning, and consider public comments with an open mind. An agency can keep its proposal even if many disagree, but if commenters raise critical new points it may publish a revised proposal or change the final rule when changes are a logical outgrowth of what was proposed. Comment text and data become part of the rulemaking record courts review.
citations: APA: agency must consider comments with open mind, may change if logical outgrowth [Hastings Center 2026]
FTC: public comments important way agency hears direct, reads and considers all when deciding what to do next [FTC 2026]
OSHA: agency considers stakeholder comments during development of final rule [OSHA 2026]

reasons.title: Short window, concrete stakes
reasons.text: Comments close Aug 31, 2026. After that USCIS reviews and issues a final rule. Filings already hit record levels in 2025 ahead of Sept 30 2026 RIA grandfathering cutoff and Jan 1 2027 inflation adjustment. Decisions now affect capital re-release, redeployment risk for India/China backlogs, and source-of-funds burden like proving origin of every dollar and exchanger license exceptions.
citations: IMI: public comment through Aug 31 2026 [IMI]
IMI: twin deadlines Sep 30 2026 grandfathering, Jan 1 2027 inflation, record filings [IMI]

why_comment.how_it_works: Agencies publish a draft, you submit a comment on regulations.gov with docket USCIS-2026-0100 explaining your concern, data, and a better approach if you have one. The agency reads all comments before issuing a final rule. You do not need to hire counsel to file; a clear personal experience with specific section numbers is useful.
what_to_include: Which provision affects you (e.g., IV.D.6 sustainment, IV.D.7 bridge financing, IV.B definitions)
Are you pre-rule or post-rule filer, conditional resident, pending I-526/829, or future investor
Real timeline or cost impact if rule stays as written
Suggested text if you have it — agencies often adopt precise regulatory language from commenters
why_comment.note: Not legal advice. Informational explainer linking to official sources.
